definition.text: Using products and services in ways that keep their harm to the environment as small as possible.

facts.text: It covers decisions across the whole consumption cycle, from choosing and using products to disposing of them, to meet present needs with the least harm to environment, economy, society and culture.
It includes buying sustainable products, avoiding unsustainable ones, and extending product life through reuse and recycling.
Food systems cause about one third of global human-made greenhouse gas emissions, so shifting to more sustainable diets is part of it.
High-income people have larger energy footprints; the top 10% consume 56% of vehicle fuel, while the bottom half causes under 20% of energy footprints.
The 1992 Earth Summit recognized it as a concept in chapter 4 of Agenda 21.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 aims to 'ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns'.
Studies find that systemic change, not just individual ethical choices, is needed for a large effect on global warming.

title: Strong and weak sustainable consumption
article: Sustainable consumption#Strong and weak sustainable consumption

definition.text: A distinction between consumption that actively cuts environmental impact (strong) and consumption that fails to (weak).

facts.text: Strong sustainable consumption means choosing renewable, efficient goods and services, such as cycling or renewable energy, and reducing living space and consumption rates.
Weak sustainable consumption includes highly polluting habits such as frequent car use and buying non-biodegradable goods.
Research found people asked to cut energy use make only minimal sacrifices and fall short of strong sustainable consumption.

title: World3

definition.text: A system dynamics computer model simulating how population, industrial growth, food production and Earth's ecosystem limits interact.

facts.text: It was built for the Club of Rome study behind The Limits to Growth (1972) by project manager Dennis Meadows and 16 researchers, extending Jay Forrester's World2.
It assumes non-renewable resources are finite and get harder to extract, diverting a growing share of industrial capital to resource extraction.
Its reference run had world population peaking at seven billion in 2030 and persistent pollution peaking in 2035 at 11 times 1970s levels.
Donella Meadows had great confidence in its qualitative conclusions but mixed confidence in its numerical parameters, some of which were 'pure guesses'.
Vaclav Smil criticized lumping very different resources and pollutants into single variables as meaningless.
A study in Yale's Journal of Industrial Ecology found data broadly consistent with its 1972 projections.

related: Limits to Growth compared with data
contested_note: Critics question the model's lumped variables and guessed parameters, while validation studies find data tracking its projections.
